title: Peak Cell in a Grid
statement:
You get an m × n grid of integers. No two cells that share a side hold the same value. Treat everything outside the grid as -1, lower than any cell.

A peak is a cell strictly greater than each of its up to four side neighbours (up, down, left, right). Return the position [row, col] of any peak. Any peak is accepted.

Aim for better than reading every cell: O(m log n) or O(n log m).

examples.why: 9 beats 4, 2 and 3. [1, 2] with 8 is also a peak (it beats 3 and 2), so either answer is accepted.
A single row rising to the right. The last cell only has a left neighbour and the -1 border.
The biggest value in a grid is always a peak, but the binary search finds one without scanning everything.

constraints: No two side-by-side cells are equal
hints: In a single row, a peak can be found by binary search: compare the middle with its right neighbour and walk uphill. Can that idea work on whole columns?
Pick the middle column and find its largest cell. That cell already beats its up and down neighbours. Only left and right are left to check.

If the left or right neighbour is bigger, a peak must exist on that side, because walking uphill from there can never cross back over the middle column's maximum. Halve the columns toward the bigger neighbour.

explain.intuition:
Take the middle column and its largest cell. Inside that column it is already a local winner, so only its left and right neighbours matter. If neither is bigger, it is a peak. If, say, the right neighbour is bigger, then the right half must hold a peak: start at that bigger cell and keep stepping to any larger neighbour. Values strictly rise, so the walk ends at a peak, and it can never step back into the middle column, because every cell there is at most the column maximum, which is smaller than where you already are.

So each step throws away half of the columns, like binary search on a 1-D array, with a column scan of O(m) per step.
steps: While lo <= hi: let mid be the middle column and r the row of its largest value.
Read left and right neighbours of grid[r][mid], using -1 off the grid.
If the cell beats both, return [r, mid]. If the right one is bigger, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Taking any cell of the middle column instead of its maximum. Then the up and down neighbours are not covered and the halving argument breaks.
Comparing only with the right neighbour like the 1-D version and returning the column max when it is not bigger. It also has to beat the left neighbour.
Forgetting the border rule: an edge cell only needs to beat the neighbours that exist.

solutions.title: Check every cell
solutions.idea: Scan the grid and return the first cell that beats all its neighbours. Simple, but it reads the whole grid.

solutions.title: Binary search over columns
solutions.idea: Take the maximum of the middle column. If a side neighbour is bigger, a peak lies on that side; otherwise this cell is a peak.

followups: Why does the same trick fail if you pick an arbitrary cell of the middle column instead of its maximum?
Binary search over whichever dimension is longer. How does that change the bound?
